summary: Defines BUNDLE, an SDP grouping extension that lets several media streams, such as audio and video, share a single transport port pair instead of using one each. This reduces the number of network resources and NAT bindings needed. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 9143.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of sending each toy in its own separate box, you pack many toys into one big box and send it once. That saves effort and fewer doors need to be opened. This version was replaced by RFC 9143.

questions: how to send audio and video over one port
what is the mid rtp header extension
subtitle: How SDP endpoints agree to send audio, video and more over one shared transport instead of one per stream.

tldr.problem: When each media stream in an SDP offer/answer gets its own transport (5-tuple), every one consumes extra resources, especially when ICE is used.
tldr.mechanism: The BUNDLE grouping extension lets an offerer and answerer negotiate one BUNDLE transport for several "m=" sections, with a bundle-only attribute and a MID identifier so received RTP can be matched to the right media description.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8843 was obsoleted by RFC 9143, which is the current BUNDLE specification.

today: RFC 8843 has been obsoleted by RFC 9143, which is now the definition of the BUNDLE extension. It updated RFC 3264, RFC 5888 and RFC 7941.

sections.title: Why Bundle Media on One Transport
sections.content:
When SDP offer/answer is used to set up a multimedia session and each media stream gets its own transport (a 5-tuple of source address, source port, destination address, destination port and transport protocol), every transport uses extra resources. This is especially true with ICE. So it is attractive to use a single transport for several media streams.

RFC 8843 defines the BUNDLE extension to the SDP Grouping Framework. The address and port an endpoint uses for the shared transport is the BUNDLE address:port, and all bundled RTP-based media belong to a single RTP session. A given BUNDLE address:port MUST be associated with only one BUNDLE group, and an offer or answer may contain several groups that are handled independently.

The extension is backward compatible: an endpoint that does not support it simply sends offers and answers without a group:BUNDLE attribute and gives each "m=" section its own address and port. It applies only to SDP used with offer/answer, not to declarative use.
sections.plainLanguage: Mailing three letters means three trips to three mailboxes. Bundling puts all three in one envelope and makes one trip.

sections.title: The Group and the bundle-only Attribute
sections.content:
A BUNDLE group is a set of "m=" sections (media descriptions) that share one BUNDLE transport. It is announced with an SDP group attribute whose semantics value is BUNDLE, followed by the identification-tags (the mid values) of the bundled sections. An "m=" section MUST NOT be in more than one BUNDLE group at a time.

The first tag in the list is the BUNDLE-tag. It points to the tagged "m=" section, whose address:port and transport-level attributes (the BUNDLE attributes) apply to every section in the group. The offerer picks a suggested offerer-tagged section, and the answerer selects the offerer-tagged and answerer-tagged sections.

The new media-level bundle-only attribute has no value. Combined with a zero port, it asks the answerer to accept that "m=" section only if it supports BUNDLE and keeps the section in the group. A zero port without bundle-only means the section is being disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The first name on the guest list is the person whose address is used for the whole group. Everyone else on the list just says, "I am with them."

sections.title: Offer and Answer Procedures
sections.content:
In an initial BUNDLE offer, the offerer gives each bundled "m=" section a unique address:port, except bundle-only sections. It picks one section as the suggested offerer-tagged section, includes a group:BUNDLE attribute, and lists every bundled section's tag, with the suggested one first. The suggested section MUST NOT be a bundle-only section, and it should be one the answerer is unlikely to reject.

The answerer may only bundle sections that the offer marked as bundled. It selects the tagged sections, gives the answerer BUNDLE address:port to the answerer-tagged section, and puts bundle-only and a zero port on every other bundled section. If it does not want to keep a section in the group, it MUST either move it out of the group or reject it. The group exists once the answerer sends the initial BUNDLE answer.

After that, offerers and answerers can add a section to the group, move one out, or disable one. In a subsequent offer or an answer, the BUNDLE attributes appear only in the tagged section. The rules for "c=" lines require the network type IN and the same address type, IP4 or IP6, in every section.
sections.plainLanguage: One side suggests who the group leader is and who is in the group. The other side agrees, changes the plan, or says some members cannot come.

sections.title: RTP, ICE and DTLS Rules
sections.content:
All RTP-based media in a BUNDLE group share one RTP session and one SSRC numbering space, and symmetric RTP MUST be used. The proto value in each bundled RTP section MUST be identical. A payload type value can be reused in several sections only if the codec configuration is identical. A given SSRC MUST NOT send packets with payload types from different bundled sections.

Because the address and port no longer identify the section, received RTP and RTCP are matched using the new MID identifier, carried as an RTCP SDES item and an RTP header extension (urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:mid). Implementations MUST support it, and the header extension MUST be enabled in each bundled RTP section in every offer and answer. Legacy peers may match by payload type instead, which requires unique payload types per section.

With ICE, connectivity checks and keepalives are needed only for the BUNDLE transport. With DTLS, there can be only one DTLS association for the group, and a DTLS client that supports DTLS-SRTP MUST include the use_srtp extension in its ClientHello. For telling STUN, DTLS and SRTP apart on one UDP transport, the RFC relies on the mechanism in RFC 5764.
sections.plainLanguage: When many kinds of mail arrive through one door, each piece needs a name label so the right person gets it. That label is the MID.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BUNDLE does not change what information flows, but it changes which addresses and ports it flows to. Streams that were once separate can end up sharing one security context. If different security policies would have applied to different streams, extra analysis is needed before bundling.

Identification-tag values MUST be generated in a way that does not leak user information, for example randomly or from a per-group counter, and SHOULD be 3 bytes or less so they fit the MID header extension. Different generation methods could allow fingerprinting of an implementation. Integrity matters, since the tag routes media to the right application function. Existing SRTP configurations protect whole RTP and RTCP packets. The RFC also adds an exception to RFC 7941: the requirement to confidentiality-protect an SDES header extension MAY be ignored for the MID extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting everything in one box means everyone who can open the box sees everything. Name tags should be random so they do not give away secrets about who you are.

sections.title: A Known Inconsistency With JSEP
sections.content:
The RFC openly records a contradiction found before publication. The JSEP document (RFC 8829) says bundle-only sections should use port zero plus a=bundle-only in initial offers only. BUNDLE says to mark them that way in all offers and answers. Most browsers at the time marked no section with port zero and used the same port for all bundled sections, while some followed JSEP.

Rather than delay publication, the documents were released as originally approved, and the IETF stated it intended to restart work and publish revised versions once a resolution was available.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rulebooks gave slightly different instructions for one situation. The authors admitted it in writing and promised to fix it later.
